Three robot bets: where does the generalization ceiling come from?

Figure, Generalist and Physical Intelligence each bet on a different source of robot generalization: the body, the data or the mix. A long read with a pinned blackboard.

October 23, 202633 min read

roboticsrobot-learningfoundation-modelshumanoids

Suppose you want a robot that can tidy a stranger's kitchen, one it has never seen, with someone else's mugs, drawers and mess on the counter. Robot people call that generalization, and three of the best-funded robot companies, Figure, Generalist and Physical Intelligence (Pi), all say it's the whole game. They just disagree about where it comes from.

Figure builds a humanoid and pays people to film themselves doing chores. Generalist hands people a cheap two-finger gripper and records them using it, more than half a million hours so far. Pi trains one model on many different robots, then lets it practice on the job. Each of these is a bet on where the generalization ceiling is: the point where putting more data and money into the approach you picked stops making the robot better in places it hasn't seen.

The question I kept coming back to is whether you need a human-shaped robot to learn from human data. Figure's answer is yes. If the answer is no, a simpler robot on wheels might be enough for a lot of homes.

Count your nines first

I took the idea of a ceiling from a talk by Dmitri Dolgov, Waymo's co-CEO and before that its CTO, at Y Combinator's Startup School in July 2026: The Demo Is Only 1% Of The Work. His point is that reliability comes in nines, 90%, 99%, 99.9%, and that each one costs far more than the last:

"getting to that first 90% or 99%, that's the easy part. But then every next nine that you want to add, that takes about 10 times more effort. So you need to know up front exactly how many nines your product actually needs." (11:46)

Every technology, he says, has a performance-versus-effort curve that starts steep and then flattens, and the common mistake is "picking the tech that gives you the fastest early ramp" and then "hitting the plateau and discovering that the technology path that you picked actually flattens out way before the performance that is required by your product" (15:16). His first example is sensing. People drive with eyes alone, so cameras are "a very reasonable way to go" for a product that only has to match people. But for strongly superhuman driving, "weak sensing just leads to a safety curve that flattens out way too early" (16:34). He showed a clip from a dust storm in Phoenix where the camera sees very little and the lidar shows a pedestrian at the side of the road (17:55). More camera data can't fix that, because the pedestrian isn't in the pixels.

His second example is learning, and it's closer to robots. Imitation with a black-box end-to-end model "will give you very rapid progress and you will ride that very initial steep part of the curve", and "for some products that's enough". But in a safety-critical product that has to beat people, "just doing kind of that basic vanilla end-to-end is not enough" (31:58). I'll call that his imitation plateau.

So what does counting nines look like for a home robot? Let's do a back-of-the-napkin calculation. Say it does 50 small tasks a day. At 99% per task it gets something wrong about every two days. To fail less than once a month it needs about 99.93% per task, and once a year takes about 99.995%. So the product needs three to four nines, and it needs them in homes nobody tested in. For each company, then, the question is what's missing from its data, or from its robot, that no amount of scale puts back.

Three bets on the ceiling

Here's how I'd put each bet in one line. Figure thinks the ceiling is the body: people are the biggest source of physical know-how, and a robot gets the most out of their data if it's shaped like them. Generalist thinks it's the data: one kind of data, real interaction recorded with the action in it, collected at enormous volume and fed to a big model. Pi thinks it's the mix: many kinds of robot data, from many robots, homes and tasks, with the robot's own practice on top.

The bets also differ on where people and robots meet. Figure reshapes the robot to fit people. Generalist reshapes people's tools to fit the robot. Pi reshapes neither and asks one model to absorb the difference.

Figure builds every layer

Figure has the most complete theory of how to win, in the sense that it has a plan for every layer. In its All Hands 2026 meeting, which it posted publicly on October 22, CEO Brett Adcock split the job into four chapters. Robot hardware and the AI recipe are problems he says "money can't buy". Scaling intelligence and scaling robots are problems money can buy. "You've got to complete all four chapters. And you can't skip chapters." (7:19)

Figure designs almost the whole robot itself, "including the actuators, motors, sensors, battery pack, and electronics" (Figure), and builds it in its own factory, BotQ, which reached a rate of one Figure 03, its current humanoid, per hour in April 2026 (Figure; Adcock said they'd build 55 that week). When it left its collaboration with OpenAI in February 2025, Adcock's reason was the same logic applied to software: "We can't outsource AI for the same reason we don't outsource actuators, batteries, or electronics" (X). And the money is there: more than $1 billion in its Series C at a $39 billion post-money valuation in September 2025 (Figure), more than $2 billion of cash now according to the all-hands (54:35), and a deal with Nscale for up to 100,000 GPUs from 2027 (Figure).

I admire this, and it isn't integration for its own sake. It serves Figure's plan to learn from people, and the hand is the clearest case. Adcock says they spent "an enormous amount of time" getting the robot's fingertips to track a person's "at millimeter level precision" (20:09). You can only shape a hand around human data if you build the hand yourself.

Two ways to meet the data

Then Adcock gets to what he calls "the largest debate in robotics the next few years", and he compares it to lidar versus cameras (18:09). His slide shows a fork with two roads. On the left, "design human collect for our robot": build specialized hardware that people use to collect data, then design the robot around that hardware. He says "there are groups out there doing it now", that the road is fun, fast and shiny, "and it will have the lowest ceiling." On the right, "design our robot for human collect": record raw human behavior and build a body that can use it, "which means the body and the hands and the way the robot moves the world over time needs to match human movements" (19:26). "It's the hardest path," he says, and it "has a much higher ceiling, maybe even unbounded ceiling."

He doesn't name them, but the left road matches what Generalist does. Then he turns to robots that work at a table:

"There are other really capable folks working on AI for robotics that I think have a really much lower ceiling and they're doing it at a tabletop. [...] They don't leave the table and the work's got to come to them and they collect millions of hours on a table." (23:34)

"And let me be clear, if you collect millions of hours on a table, you will generalize to a table and you'll pick up balls and do other stuff. [...] You have to generalize to that over there on the right. And then when you start generalizing to that, you're going to have to re-architect everything here on the left. I've been there. We've been on a table before, and we hit a wall." (24:03)

He doesn't name anyone here either, and I don't know of anyone with millions of hours on a table yet, so I read it as a description of a strategy more than of one company. Read closely, the claim is also narrower than I remembered it. He doesn't say that table data is useless once the robot walks. He says table data generalizes to tables, that leaving the table means re-architecting everything, and that Figure had to leave the table itself: "It's not a manipulation problem. It's not a tabletop problem. It's a whole body problem." The year he describes went into rebuilding Helix, Figure's robot model, so that it sends commands "to every joint": "We had to re-architect Helix to be able to do this, and it took a year." (26:05) So the wall Figure hit was partly in its own model, and it doesn't show by itself that table data can't transfer.

So is the humanoid the only way to win? Adcock's answer is yes. The body has to match human movement so it can learn from human data, and "post-training is not going to win this game. It's pre-training that will win." (50:14) There are two claims folded into that. One is that raw human data has a higher ceiling than data collected with robot-shaped tools. The other is that only a human-shaped robot can use human data, and that's the claim that makes the humanoid necessary. So what has Figure tested?

Figure's test: 30 homes it never saw

Figure's best evidence came a month before the all-hands. For Helix 2.5 it took robots into 30 Bay Area homes "with zero data collected in any of them." The tasks were still taught with robot data from elsewhere. Figure's own note says ""Zero-shot" refers to the evaluation environments and objects being manipulated; tasks were specified through fine-tuning data collected elsewhere." The model was "pretrained from random initialization entirely on Index", Figure's dataset of human video, with no vision-language model underneath. That's a turn from the first Helix in February 2025, which sat on a 7B-parameter vision-language model and about 500 hours of robot data.

Then Figure ran a controlled comparison. Holding the task data, the model, the training and the test fixed, it measured the robot with and without Index pretraining, on three household tasks with 140 trials each. Success went from 12 to 87 on folding towels, 7 to 56 on picking up toys and 16 to 94 on making a bed. Pooled, that's 35 of 420 against 237 of 420, so 8% against 56%. (The post's text says 9%, but its own counts give 8%.)

That's the strongest public result I found, from any of the three companies, that human video makes a robot better in places it hasn't seen. It's Figure's own test and it isn't peer reviewed, and 56% still means 44 failures in a hundred. It also doesn't touch the part of the bet that needs a humanoid. There's no robot without a human shape in the comparison, so it shows that human video helps Figure's humanoid, not that a different body couldn't get the same lift. The same goes for Project Go-Big in 2025, where Helix learned to walk through homes from "100% egocentric human video data", meaning video from cameras worn by people, and "no robot demonstrations whatsoever". Figure published no success rate for it, so I count it as a demo. Meanwhile Index keeps growing: Adcock's slide says 37.5 million videos from 112 countries, and he estimates Figure spent $8.1 million on data in one week (43:50, 46:18).

Generalist: robot-shaped data from human hands

My prior on Generalist was that its edge is better pretraining from collecting much more data. That's partly right, but the data is a different kind than I assumed.

The volume part is real. Generalist was incorporated in 2024, with Pete Florence, Andrew Barry and Andy Zeng as its executive officers (SEC Form D), and in June 2026 it raised $400 million, bringing its total to "more than half a billion dollars" (Generalist). A second filing in August shows about $198 million more sold (SEC Form D). Florence describes a grad-school experiment where he strapped a GoPro to his head, held two clamps as if they were robot grippers and walked around the lab, and he says it showed a path to "vastly more data than we ever have had in robotics before" (podcast, 11:13). In November 2025 Generalist reported more than 270,000 hours, growing by 10,000 hours a week (GEN-0), and by April 2026 "over half a million hours" (GEN-1).

That data isn't robot data, though. People hold "low-cost wearable devices", hand-held two-finger grippers with a camera, built to match the robot's own gripper. Barry, the CTO, says "we couldn't find the grippers that kind of matched the type of data collection we wanted to do", and that it's "all about making sure the data set and the inference time matches" (podcast, 27:38). Generalist says the base models of both GEN-0 and GEN-1 are "trained without any robot data". The robot shows up only after pretraining, with about an hour of robot data per task.

The founders also don't describe the edge as hours. "Data is incredibly important and it is table stakes," Florence said in October (podcast, 35:50), and "an hour of data is not a fungible unit" (38:45). They say the hand-held data keeps a person's natural, fast movement, which teleoperation, driving a robot by remote control, loses: a post by Andy Zeng and the Generalist team calls teleoperated trajectories "stiff and stilted" (Generalist). They say the model has to be big enough to absorb it: in their GEN-0 tests a 1B-parameter model showed "ossification", meaning it stopped taking in new data, while larger models kept improving. And they test data mixtures to learn which data helps most. So my corrected prior is that the bet is a large volume of one well-chosen kind of data, a model big enough to use it, and a fast way to find out which data matters.

Their results are about how little robot data a new task needs. With about one hour of robot data per task, GEN-1 reached 99% average success on three tasks, against 64% for GEN-0 and 19% for a model trained from scratch (GEN-1). GEN-1.5 got 83% across 10 simple, short tasks after 10 training steps on five minutes of data per task, about 50 demonstrations. These are trained tasks rather than new homes, the averages come without trial counts or a paper, and nothing is released. Academic results with the same kind of device are strong too: one study reached 85% to 92.5% success on four tasks in eight unseen places with unseen objects, with no robot data at all (Lin et al.).

On the hand, Generalist's view is the opposite of Figure's. A July post says "Hands can change, physics does not," and that with a general enough model "the shape of the hand becomes secondary to the intelligence that drives it" (Generalist). It still treats the question as open: Florence calls generalizing to new hands "not quite solved" (interview, 18:44).

Physical Intelligence: one model, many bodies

Pi's bet is the least about one body. Its founders say the only route to generalization they know is variety. "The only answer to generalization that we know in machine learning is through diversity of data," co-founder Karol Hausman said in a Sequoia interview released in January (interview, 7:42). In Pi's published models, most of that variety comes from robots: many robots, many places and many tasks in one model.

The clearest measured case is π0.5, the model from the 2025 videos of a robot cleaning homes it had never seen. It used about 400 hours of data from its target robots, two-armed robots on wheels, in about 100 homes, and Pi says 97.6% of the training examples in the first training phase didn't come from those robots doing household tasks. They came from other robots, static arms set up in homes, and the web. On Pi's blog chart, success with unseen objects was 94% with everything, 31% without the static arms in homes, 49% without the other lab robots and 74% without the web data. In the paper, a model trained on 104 locations did about as well in the test homes as a control trained in those homes.

Pi doesn't skip hardware, which surprised me. A job post from October says "We design and build our own robots" at "our factory in Fremont" (Pi). They're simple robots, mostly two-armed, all with parallel-jaw grippers, on wheels or fixed in place. Sergey Levine says they've stayed away from humanoids for data collection, and "it's not ideological, it's just because humanoids are expensive, complicated, and teleoperating humanoids is harder" (interview, 46:11). Partners already run Pi's models on their own humanoids through its API, so for Pi the body is a variable, not a commitment. Pi hasn't posted its funding. CapitalG, which led its Series B in November 2025, lists the round at $600 million on its insights page.

The third part of the bet is practice. A VLA, or vision-language-action model, is a robot policy built on a model of images and text, and both Figure's Helix and Pi's models are described that way. Pi's blog puts Dolgov's imitation plateau in robot terms: "it's relatively easy to get VLAs to succeed at a task some of the time, it's quite hard to make them succeed reliably." Its answer, a method called Recap, trains on the robot's own attempts and on people's corrections, and "On some of the hardest tasks, RECAP more than doubles task throughput and roughly halves the task failure rate" (paper), where throughput means successful runs per hour. In April, π0.7 folded that practice back into one general model, which did about as well as the specialists trained by practice.

On human data, Pi sits between the other two. Levine's essay Sporks of AGI argues that human video, hand-held grippers and simulation each represent "a compromise" in the limit, because a model trained on human data "will try to predict how a human will approach this problem, rather than predicting an effective strategy for a robot." He wants that data to "supplement rather than replace" real experience on the robot. Pi's human-to-robot paper then found that a few hours of human data per task do help, but only on top of a model pretrained on varied robot data. With little or no pretraining, "VLAs cannot benefit from human data co-training", co-training meaning mixing the human data into the robot training.

Pi's evidence has gaps too. The π0.5 home tests ran 10 trials per task and home, and for its newer models Pi gives only a rough size, "tens of thousands of hours of demonstrations" in the π*0.6 paper, so "variety beats volume" is hard to check against the size of the data.

Human data on robots that aren't human-shaped

Now the question from the start: do you need a human body to use human data? For the amounts of human data tested so far, the published results say no. Human data gives measured gains on robots that look nothing like people: arms with two-finger grippers, two-armed robots on wheels, robots that only drive. Pi's human-to-robot paper is one example. People wore a head camera, and in some runs wrist cameras, and repeated the robot's tasks while their head and hand motion was tracked. Three hours of this data raised a two-armed gripper robot on wheels from 32% to 71% on a spice-rack task, in a kitchen it had seen only in the human data. EMMA, on another two-armed robot on wheels, never drove the robot around to collect data. On one task, demos of the robot standing still plus one hour of video of people walking and doing the task reached 82%, against 52% for a standard model trained on one hour of the robot driven by remote control.

The biggest gains on the board are on humanoids, HAT's +25 points and EgoHumanoid's +51, so a humanoid with hands can clearly use human data. The real question is whether it gains more than other bodies would, and the few papers that compare bodies don't show that. ImMimic gave the same 100 human videos per task to one arm fitted with four different hands. With the authors' method, which maps human hand motion onto each hand, its two grippers gained 26 points of average success and its two dexterous hands gained 25. With plain co-training the hands gained more, 16 points against 6. The authors find that the gain tracks how close the human actions are to the robot's, "regardless of its mechanical structure", and conclude that "More human-mimetic embodiments don't necessarily lead to better transfer." EgoVerse gave two gripper arms and a Unitree G1 humanoid with hands a shared 8-hour human dataset plus 2 hours recorded in each lab's scene, and the humanoid's gains fell inside the range of the two gripper setups.

What hurts is misalignment. On one task in the What Matters study, human video doubled success over robot-only data, 26.2% to 51.2%, once the human camera's image scale was matched to the robot's, and with a badly mismatched camera it added nothing (25.0%). Grasp style points the same way. When people hold a cup in a way the gripper can't copy, plain imitation with the human data fell below the robot-only baseline, from 25% to 15% in EgoWAM, though with 20 trials that drop is within noise. So some of what human data teaches survives a change of body, and some doesn't. Scenes, objects, the order of a task, where to go and roughly where the hand goes all carry over to a gripper on wheels. Grasp style, finger contact and whole-body motion don't, and fine precision is a weak point, since hand-tracking labels carry 1 to 2 cm of error (EgoZero). Whole-body motion is the one part only a humanoid can use, by mapping human motion capture onto its joints.

There's one tension these papers can't resolve. Most of them mix a few hours of human data into robot training, and Pi found that a small amount helps only on top of varied robot pretraining. Figure's bet runs at a different scale: Helix 2.5 is pretrained on human video alone, from scratch, and it worked. Generalist also pretrains with no robot data, on human-held grippers. Nobody has run Figure's recipe on a robot without a human shape, so at that scale the body question is still open.

The other limit is sample size. Most of these comparisons run 10 to 50 trials per condition. With 10 trials, a 50% success rate is uncertain by about 31 points either way at 95% confidence. Even with 20 to 40 trials per body, a test can miss a gap of 30 to 40 points between two bodies. I'm writing up the paper-by-paper evidence in a companion article.

Legs, wheels and the flat with no stairs

Then there's the body itself. Even if a robot on wheels can learn from human video, a humanoid can climb stairs and a wheeled robot can't. Isn't that the end of it?

Dolgov's frame gives both sides a point. A wheel at a stair is a ceiling of his kind, a physical limit that no amount of data removes, the same way more camera data doesn't help when the pedestrian isn't in the pixels. If the product is "any home", that's a hard ceiling for a wheeled robot, and Figure says so: "wheeled robots need enough open floor for their base to fit and turn. Homes offer no such accommodation" (Helix 2.5). But Dolgov also called cameras alone "a very reasonable way to go" when the product only has to match people. Counting nines starts from the product. For a robot sold into flats, warehouses and offices with elevators, the stair ceiling sits above the target, and what's left is cost and the hand.

That's the Roomba argument, and I think it holds. A Roomba doesn't climb stairs either, and it sold because it was cheap and good enough on one floor. Generalist and Pi already run their models on wheels. Generalist's GTC demo used "UR7e arms on a MiR base" (Generalist), and π0.5 ran on robots with "a wheeled holonomic base, and a torso lift mechanism" (Pi), meaning a base that rolls in any direction and a body that raises and lowers its arms. I can't compare prices from primary sources. Levine says each arm on Pi's robots costs about $3,000 (interview, 1:12:46), Figure publishes no price, and Adcock describes Figure's next hand as having "more actuators than an entire robot" (16:42). I can't put a number on the gap, but I can tell which way it points.

So the two claims from Figure's fork get different answers. The body does set a hard ceiling on which tasks a robot can reach, and legs raise it. That the body also sets the ceiling on how much a robot learns from human data is the claim nobody has shown, and the comparisons that exist don't show a humanoid advantage.

Four ceilings, and who attacks which

Put together, I count at least four generalization ceilings, and the three bets push on different ones.

The body ceiling is what the robot can physically reach. It's the only hard physical limit of the four, and Figure's bet is the only one going after it. How much it matters depends on the tasks in your product.

The data ceiling is what the data covers and what it contains, and all three push on it by trading one for the other. Human video covers the most situations and contains the least per hour, with no actions and no forces, so Figure has to estimate the hand motion and build a hand that can follow it. Generalist's grippers record the action directly, since the person is moving a copy of the robot's own hand, and the price is a robot with a pincer. Pi's robot data contains the robot's exact actions and covers less, which is why it mixes so many sources.

The demonstrator ceiling is Dolgov's imitation plateau: copying gets a robot close to the people it copies, and reliability takes something more. Pi has the clearest measured answer, a robot that practices and gets corrected. Generalist says GEN-1 also learns "from experience (RL)" (GEN-1). Figure's all-hands puts the weight at the other end: "It's pre-training that will win."

The evaluation ceiling gets talked about least. You can't climb nines you can't measure. If a robot succeeds 3,000 times in a row, you can say with 95% confidence that it fails less than 0.1% of the time, which statisticians call the rule of three. Put the best numbers above on Dolgov's ladder and they sit around one nine or below in new places or with new things: Figure's 56% in 30 new homes, π0.5's 94% with unseen objects, and π0.7's 60% to 80% on tasks or robot pairings it hadn't seen (π0.7 paper). Generalist's 99% is two nines, on three tasks it was trained for. A home robot needs three or four nines, and nobody has published a test big enough to show them.

Figure's question is the right one, and its answer goes further than its evidence. Figure has the best public evidence that human video helps a robot in new homes, and the body does set a hard ceiling on what a robot can reach. But the claim that you need a humanoid to learn from human data is the one part of its argument it hasn't tested. Video gives you the most data, and it doesn't need the exact body. It needs a hand and a camera that line up with it.

I also don't buy "the lowest ceiling" for Generalist's road. It gives up some breadth to get the action into the data, and the hand-held results so far, Generalist's and the academic ones, are among the best numbers in this whole comparison. Pi's bet is the closest to Dolgov's point about real-world experience: data from the robots you ship, from as many places as possible, then practice until the failures go away. The match is only partial, since Dolgov also puts heavy weight on simulation and on structure built into the model.

If I had to pick the highest ceiling, I wouldn't pick a body. I'd pick whoever turns a robot's own experience into training data fastest, on a body chosen for the product. That's a bet, and the evidence for it is thinner than for anything else here: Recap's halved failure rate, π0.7 matching the specialists trained by practice, and Dolgov saying about cars that "the actual experience of having your agent in the real world is invaluable and it's irreplaceable" (5:59). But three of the four ceilings rise when a robot can learn from its own attempts, and the fourth is the body. In a house with stairs, the right body is probably a humanoid. In a flat, I think a simpler robot on wheels with a good hand wins, the way the Roomba did.

Here's the comparison in one place.

Main data human video (Index) hand-held grippers, over 500,000 hours many robots, homes and tasks, then practice
Headline result new homes: 8% to 56% with human video pretraining trained tasks, about 1 hour of robot data each: 99% unseen objects: 94%, and 31% without the static arms in homes

Tasks, labs and metrics differ between papers, so the dots don't compare directly.

Left out because I couldn't verify them. A price for Figure 03, and the valuations of Generalist and Pi, which only news reports give.

The napkin numbers. 50 tasks a day at 99% success gives 0.5 failures a day, one every two days. At 99.9% it's one every 20 days. One failure a month is 1 in 1,500 tasks, so 99.93%, and one a year is 1 in 18,250, so about 99.995%. For 10 trials at 50%, the 95% interval is about ±1.96 × √(0.5 × 0.5 / 10), or ±31 points. To detect a difference between two bodies from a 50% baseline (two-sided test at 5%, 80% power) takes about 20 trials each for 40 points, 40 for 30 points and 60 for 25 points. The rule of three: with zero failures in nnn trials, the 95% upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/n3/n3/n, so 3,000 clean trials bound it at 0.1%.
